title: Bubble, Selection and Insertion Sort
excerpt: Three quadratic sorts that look interchangeable and are not. One of them is genuinely useful in production, and it is not the one people expect.
seoTitle: Bubble vs Selection vs Insertion Sort: What Actually Differs
seoDescription: Three O(n^2) sorts compared properly: writes, stability, adaptivity, and why insertion sort is the only one that survives into production code.

content.text: All three of these are O(n²) and all three are taught together, which gives the impression they are the same algorithm with cosmetic differences. They are not. They differ in how many writes they do, whether they notice sorted input, and whether they are stable, and those differences decide which one survives into real code.
Walk the array comparing neighbors and swapping any that are out of order, and after one pass the largest value has been carried to the end. Repeat.

Its one redeeming feature is the early exit: if a whole pass makes no swaps, the array is sorted and you can stop. That makes it O(n) on already-sorted input. Without that check it is O(n²) unconditionally, and the version without the check is the one most people write.
Switch the input to "already sorted" and watch it stop after a single pass with zero writes.
Find the smallest remaining value, swap it into place, repeat. The comparison count is fixed at n(n-1)/2 no matter what, because it always scans the whole remaining array.

What it does have is the fewest writes of any of these: exactly n-1 swaps, regardless of the input. If comparisons are cheap and writes are expensive, which is the case for flash memory or for records that are large to move, that is a real advantage.
It is not stable, and the reason is worth seeing: swapping a distant minimum into position can jump one of a pair of equal values over the other.
Grow a sorted prefix. Take the next value, slide it left past everything larger, and drop it in. This is how most people sort a hand of cards.

row underneath. While the shifting loop runs, the value being placed is out of the array entirely, held in a variable, and its old slot has been overwritten. That is why the bars briefly show a duplicate: it is real, not a rendering artifact.

Insertion sort is stable, adaptive, and in place. On nearly-sorted input each value moves only a step or two, so the inner loop barely runs and the whole thing is close to O(n). That combination is why it is the only one of the three that appears in production sorts.
Run all three on the same input using the full visualizer, and read the table at the bottom. The interesting comparisons are on the non-random presets.

questions.prompt: Which of these three is used inside real production sorts, and why?

options.label: Insertion sort, because it is fast on small and nearly-sorted inputs
Bubble sort, because of its early exit
Selection sort, because it does the fewest swaps
It does exactly n-1 swaps, which matters when writing is expensive
It is adaptive to sorted input

questions.prompt: Why do the bars briefly show a duplicate during insertion sort?

options.label: The value being inserted is held in a variable while its old slot is overwritten
It is a rendering bug in the visualizer
Insertion sort genuinely duplicates values and removes them later
